excerpts: The liberty interest at issue in this case — the interest of parents in the care, custody, and control of their children— is perhaps the oldest of the fundamental liberty interests recognized by this Court.

Section 26.10.160(B) of the Revised Code of Washington permits “[a]ny person” to petition a superior court for visitation rights “at any time,” and authorizes that court to grant such visitation rights whenever “visitation may serve the best interest of the child.” Petitioners Jenifer and Gary Troxel petitioned a Washington Superior Court for the right to visit their grandchildren, Isabelle and Natalie Troxel. Respondent Tommie Granville, the mother of Isabelle and Natalie, opposed the petition.

The Washington Supreme Court nevertheless agreed with the Court of Appeals’ ultimate conclusion that the Troxels could not obtain visitation of Isabelle and Natalie pursuant to §26.10.160(3). The court rested its decision on the Federal Constitution, holding that §26.10.160(3) unconstitutionally infringes on the fundamental right of parents to rear their children. In the court’s view, there were at least two problems with the nonparental visitation statute. First, according to the Washington Supreme Court, the Constitution permits a State to interfere with the right of parents to rear their children only to prevent harm or potential harm to a child.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-133-f3d-631.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-133-f3d-631.summary: The court applied the fundamental right to marry under the Fourteenth Amendment. It held that the city’s termination of Singleton based on his wife’s conduct did not directly or substantially interfere with, or significantly discourage, the marriage and therefore did not violate substantive due process.
excerpts: Singleton claims that his termination violated his substantive due process right of privacy in his marital relationship. The fundamental right of privacy embodies the “principle that personal decisions that profoundly affect bodily integrity, identity, and destiny should be largely beyond the reach of government.” Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833, 927, 112 S.Ct. 2791, 2846, 120 L.Ed.2d 674 (1992) (Blackmun, J., concurring in part, concurring in the judgment in part, and dissenting in part). The Supreme Court has recognized “that the right to marry is part of the fundamental ‘right of privacy implicit in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process clause.” Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U.S. 374, 384, 98 S.Ct. 673, 680, 54 L.Ed.2d 618 (1977).

This right, however, does not invalidate every state action that has some impact on marriage. See Gorrie v. Bowen, 809 F.2d 508, 522-23 (8th Cir.1987) (“Not every regulation that involves or somehow regulates on the basis of family membership is unconstitutional.”). Rather, the government is free to impose “reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into the marital relationship____” Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 386, 98 S.Ct. at 681. Government action “must interfere ‘directly and substantially5 with family choices before it is unconstitutional,” Gorrie, 809 F.2d at 523 (quoting Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 387, 98 S.Ct. at 681) (citation omitted), but action having only a collateral effect on family decisions typically does not violate that right.

us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.citation: Whisman ex rel. Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303 (8th Cir. 1997)
us-ca8-119-f3d-1303.summary: The court held that parents possess a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, and that parents and children have a corresponding liberty interest in familial association. The alleged removal and continued retention of the child without reasonable suspicion of abuse or a prompt post-deprivation hearing stated a due-process claim.
excerpts: Michelle has alleged that defendants’ actions violated her constitutional right to not be deprived of the custody of her son without due process of law. Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.1987). Both parents and children have a liberty interest in the care and companionship of each other.

Even if defendants had a right to take temporary custody of Joel, defendants had a corresponding obligation to afford Michelle and Joel an adequate post-deprivation hearing. Doe v. Hennepin County, 858 F.2d 1325, 1329 (8th Cir.1988). The right to an adequate post-deprivation hearing was clearly established in February of 1995.

us-scotus-519-102.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-519-102.summary: The Court held that Mississippi could not condition an appeal from a parental-rights termination decree on an indigent parent’s prepayment of record-preparation fees. Because the State had authorized appellate review and the proceeding involved the permanent severance of a fundamental parent-child relationship, denying review solely because of poverty violated the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: By order of a Mississippi Chancery Court, petitioner M. L. B.’s parental rights to her two minor children were forever terminated. M. L. B. sought to appeal from the termination decree, but Mississippi required that she pay in advance record preparation fees estimated at $2,352.36. Because M. L. B. lacked funds to pay the fees, her appeal was dismissed. was Urging that the size of her pocketbook should not be dis-positive when “an interest far more precious than any property right” is at stake, Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U. S. 745, 758-759 (1982), M. L. B. tenders this question, which we agreed to hear and decide: May a State, consistent with the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, condition appeals from trial court decrees terminating parental rights on the affected parent’s ability to pay record preparation fees? We hold that, just as a State may not block an indigent petty offender’s access to an appeal afforded others, see Mayer v. Chicago, 404 U. S. 189, 195-196 (1971), so Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent.

Choices about marriage, family life, and the upbringing of children are among associational rights this Court has ranked as “of basic importance in our society,” Boddie, 401 U. S., at 376, rights sheltered by the Fourteenth Amendment against the State’s unwarranted usurpation, disregard, or disrespect. See, for example, Turner v. Safley, 482 U. S. 78 (1987), Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U. S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967) (marriage); Skinner v. Oklahoma ex rel. Williamson, 316 U. S. 535 (1942) (procreation); Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510 (1925), and Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390 (1923) (raising children). M. L. B.’s case, involving the State’s authority to sever permanently a parent-child bond, demands the close consideration the Court has long required when a family association so undeniably important is at stake.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses)

us-ca8-87-f3d-1011.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-87-f3d-1011.summary: The court recognized that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and that visitation rights may be subject to due-process scrutiny. It further held that a substantive due-process claim based on interference with visitation requires conduct that abuses official power and shocks the conscience; the court found no prior case establishing a constitutional violation at that level.
excerpts: It is beyond question that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1986) (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983), citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 753, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 1394, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)) (alteration in original). This right, however, is not absolute. Manzano v. South Dakota Dep’t of Social Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir.1995).

To the extent Zakrzewski claims a substantive due process violation of Ms parenting liberty interest, he must demonstrate that the defendants abused their official power in a manner that shocks the conscience, regardless of whether state-law remedies are available. New v. City of Minneapolis, 792 F.2d 724, 725-26 (8th Cir.1986). “[T]he theory of substantive due process is properly reserved for truly egregious and extraordinary cases,” Myers v. Scott County, 868 F.2d 1017, 1019 (8th Cir.1989),

us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.citation: Thomason v. SCAN Volunteer Services, Inc., 85 F.3d 1365 (8th Cir. 1996)
us-ca8-85-f3d-1365.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the government’s compelling interest in protecting children. In the context of a child-abuse investigation, officials are entitled to qualified immunity when an otherwise disruptive action is reasonably founded on suspicion of abuse.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991-92, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1988)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983).

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).

Clearly, our precedents provide that, when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (substantive due process)

us-ca8-70-f3d-1012.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-70-f3d-1012.summary: The court held that a child-welfare worker’s alleged failure to follow a state-court reunification plan or state agency policy did not, standing alone, establish a violation of the parent’s federal constitutional liberty interest. It affirmed qualified immunity because no clearly established constitutional right required strict adherence to the plan.
excerpts: Mr. Ebmeier claims the defendants “disregarded” both the Buffalo County Court’s order approving the reunification plan and NDSS policy, thereby violating his “constitutionally protected fundamental liberty interest in the care and custody of his children.” As the District Court put it, Mr. Ebmeier asserts a “clearly established right requiring the defendants to adhere strictly to the court order that directed them to devise a reunification plan.

It is established beyond peradventure that a state actor’s failure to observe a duty imposed by state law, standing alone, is not a sufficient foundation on which to erect a section 1983 claim. Although it is true that constitutional significance may attach to certain interests created by state law, not every transgression of state law does double duty as a constitutional violation.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-60-f3d-505.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-60-f3d-505.citation: Manzano v. South Dakota Department of Social Services, 60 F.3d 505 (8th Cir. 1995)
us-ca8-60-f3d-505.summary: The court recognized that parents have a Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children and in familial integrity. It held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the compelling governmental interest in protecting minor children, particularly during child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983). However, we have at the same time indicated that this right is not absolute.

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-scotus-495-604.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-495-604.summary: The Court held that California’s exercise of personal jurisdiction over a nonresident personally served while physically present in California was consistent with the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, even though the suit was unrelated to his activities in the State. Traditional transient-presence jurisdiction remains constitutionally permissible when process is properly served.
excerpts: Among the most firmly established principles of personal jurisdiction in American tradition is that the courts of a State have jurisdiction over nonresidents who are physically present in the State. The view developed early that each State had the power to hale before its courts any individual who could be found within its borders, and that once having acquired jurisdiction over such a person by properly serving him with process, the State could retain jurisdiction to enter judgment against him, no matter how fleeting his visit.

To determine whether the assertion of personal jurisdiction is consistent with due process, we have long relied on the principles traditionally followed by American courts in marking out the territorial limits of each State’s authority. That criterion was first announced in Pennoyer v. Neff, supra, in which we stated that due process “mean[s] a course of legal proceedings according to those rules and principles which have been established in our systems of jurisprudence for the protection and enforcement of private rights,” id., at 733, including the “well-established principles of public law respecting the jurisdiction of an independent State over persons and property,” id., at 722.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.citation: Henne ex rel. Henne v. Wright, 904 F.2d 1208 (8th Cir. 1990)
us-ca8-904-f2d-1208.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive-due-process principles to determine whether parents have a fundamental right to give a child at birth a surname lacking a legally established parental connection. It recognized constitutionally protected parental child-rearing interests but held that those interests are not absolute and do not establish the asserted naming right.
excerpts: Whether there is a fundamental right to give a child a surname at birth with which the child has no legally established parental connection will dictate the appropriate level of constitutional scrutiny for evaluating Neb.Rev.Stat. § 71-640.01. Specifically, if the statute significantly infringes a right deemed fundamental under the fourteenth amendment right of privacy then we must rigorously scrutinize the asserted justifications for the statute.

While Meyer and Pierce extended constitutional protection to parental decisions relating to child rearing, the parental rights recognized in those cases centered primarily around the training and education of children. For example, the law at issue in Meyer prevented parents from having their children taught in a foreign language, 262 U.S. at 396-403, 43 S.Ct. at 626-28, and the law at issue in Pierce prevented parents from sending their children to non-public schools, 268 U.S. at 529-36, 45 S.Ct. at 571-74.

us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.citation: Lux ex rel. Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064 (8th Cir. 1989)
us-ca8-886-f2d-1064.summary: The court applied the substantive due process principle that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It considered that asserted right in reviewing the qualified-immunity defense to the § 1983 claim arising from the child’s separation from her father.
excerpts: Carrie alleges that her due process and liberty rights were violated when she was separated from her father as a result of DSS’s investigation and the subsequent dependency and neglect proceedings. She cites Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403 (8th Cir.1986), in which we recognized that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Id. at 407 (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-491-110.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-491-110.citation: Michael H. v. Gerald D., 491 U.S. 110 (1989)
us-scotus-491-110.summary: The plurality held that California’s conclusive marital-paternity presumption was a substantive rule implementing family-integrity policy, rather than a procedural due-process defect. It rejected Michael’s claim that his biological connection and relationship with Victoria gave him a constitutionally protected liberty interest requiring recognition as her legal father or conferring parental rights against the intact marital family.
excerpts: This Court has struck down as illegitimate certain “irrebut-table presumptions.” See, e. g., Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972); Vlandis v. Kline, 412 U. S. 441 (1973); Cleveland Board of Education v. LaFleur, 414 U. S. 632 (1974). Those holdings did not, however, rest upon procedural due process. A conclusive presumption does, of course, foreclose the person against whom it is invoked from demonstrating, in a particularized proceeding, that applying the presumption to him will in fact not further the lawful governmental policy the presumption is designed to effectuate.

We therefore reject Michael’s procedural due process challenge and proceed to his substantive claim. Michael contends as a matter of substantive due process that, because he has established a parental relationship with Victoria, protection of Gerald’s and Carole’s marital union is an insufficient state interest to support termination of that relationship. This argument is, of course, predicated on the assertion that Michael has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in his relationship with Victoria.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-489-189.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-489-189.citation: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189 (1989)
us-scotus-489-189.summary: The Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment does not generally require state or local officials to protect a child from private violence by failing to remove him from a parent’s custody. The State’s knowledge of the abuse and its failure to intervene did not, on these facts, create an affirmative constitutional duty to protect Joshua.
excerpts: Petitioner is a boy who was beaten and permanently injured by his father, with whom he lived. Respondents are social workers and other local officials who received complaints that petitioner was being abused by his father and had reason to believe that this was the case, but nonetheless did not act to remove petitioner from his father’s custody. Petitioner sued respondents claiming that their failure to act deprived him of his liberty in violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. We hold that it did not.

The complaint alleged that respondents had deprived Joshua of his liberty without due process of law, in violation of his rights under the Fourteenth Amendment, by failing to intervene to protect him against a risk of violence at his father’s hands of which they knew or should have known. The District Court granted summary judgment for respondents.

The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, 812 F. 2d 298 (1987), holding that petitioners had not made out an actionable § 1983 claim for two alternative reasons. First, the court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment does not require a state or local governmental entity to protect its citizens from “private violence, or other mishaps not attributable to the conduct of its employees.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-852-f2d-1039.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-852-f2d-1039.summary: The court rejected the parents’ claim that the Fourteenth Amendment gives them a fundamental right to supervise their children’s education free from state testing requirements. It also applied rational-basis review to Arkansas’s differing regulation of home schools and private schools, upholding the classification.
excerpts: Second, we find no persuasive arguments advanced that there is a fundamental right of parents to supervise their children’s education to the extent that the Murphys contend. The recognition of such a right would fly directly in the face of those cases in which the Supreme Court has recognized the broad power of the state to compel school attendance and regulate curriculum and teacher certification. See Board of Education v. Allen, 392 U.S. at 245-46, 88 S.Ct. at 1927-28; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 534, 45 S.Ct. 571, 573, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925). Thus, again, strict scrutiny cannot be invoked in this case.

Given that strict scrutiny analysis does not apply, we move to the question of whether Arkansas has a rational reason to subject home schooling to regulatory requirements, while at the same time freeing private schools from virtually any regulation. This step by the legislature in Arkansas may at first glance offend common sense, and, sitting as a legislature, we might not have made this same decision. However, our job is not to sit as a legislature and the constitutional standard of rationality under the equal protection clause is a relaxed one.

us-scotus-486-456.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-486-456.summary: The Court applied intermediate scrutiny to Pennsylvania’s statute limiting paternity actions by children born out of wedlock. It held that such a limitation must provide a reasonable opportunity to establish paternity and must be substantially related to the State’s interest in preventing stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: To withstand intermediate scrutiny, a statutory classification must be substantially related to an important governmental objective.

In considering whether state legislation violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, U. S. Const., Arndt. 14, § 1, we apply different levels of scrutiny to different types of classifications. At a minimum, a statutory classification must be rationally related to a legitimate governmental purpose.

To withstand intermediate scrutiny, a statutory classification must be substantially related to an important governmental objective. Consequently we have invalidated classifications that burden illegitimate children for the sake of punishing the illicit relations of their parents, because “visiting this condemnation on the head of an infant is illogical and unjust.
provisions: U.S. Const., amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-485-624.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-485-624.citation: Hicks ex rel. Feiock v. Feiock, 485 U.S. 624 (1988)
us-scotus-485-624.summary: The Court treated the characterization of a contempt proceeding and its sanction as civil or criminal, for purposes of applying the Due Process Clause, as a federal-law question rather than one controlled by the State’s characterization. In this child-support enforcement proceeding, it addressed whether inability to comply was an element or affirmative defense, the allocation of proof under § 1209.5, and whether the contempt relief was civil or criminal.
excerpts: Three issues must be decided to resolve this case. First is whether the ability to comply with a court order constitutes an element of the offense of contempt or, instead, inability to comply is an affirmative defense to that charge. Second is whether § 1209.5 requires the alleged contemnor to shoulder the burden of persuasion or merely the burden of production in attempting to establish his inability to comply with the order. Third is whether this contempt proceeding was a criminal proceeding or a civil proceeding, i. e., whether the relief imposed upon respondent was criminal or civil in nature.

The third issue, however, is a different matter: the argument is not merely that the state court misapplied state law, but that the characterization of this proceeding and the relief given as civil or criminal in nature, for purposes of determining the proper applicability of federal constitutional protections, raises a question of federal law rather than state law. This proposition is correct as stated. In re Winship, 397 U. S. 358, 365-366 (1970); In re Gault, 387 U. S. 1, 49-50 (1967); Shillitani v. United States, 384 U. S. 364, 368-369 (1966). The fact that this proceeding and the resultant relief were judged to be criminal in nature as a matter of state law is thus not determinative of this issue, and the state appellate court erred insofar as it sustained respondent’s challenge to the statute under the Due Process Clause simply because it concluded that this contempt proceeding is “quasi-criminal” as a matter of California law.

us-ca8-828-f2d-493.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.citation: Estate of Brandon v. Commissioner, 828 F.2d 493 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-828-f2d-493.summary: The court held that a settlement qualifies for the estate-tax marital deduction only to the extent it reflects an enforceable surviving-spouse claim under properly interpreted state law. It remanded for an independent determination whether Arkansas’s gender-based dower-election statute was constitutional under the Equal Protection Clause at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr.
excerpts: Specifically, we agree that “under even the most narrow reading of Bosch, either a good faith settlement or a judgment of a lower state court must be based on an enforceable right, under state law properly interpreted, in order to qualify as ‘passing’ pursuant to the estate tax marital deduction.” Ahmanson, supra, 674 F.2d at 775.

Bosch and Ahmanson support the conclusion that the Tax Court was required, in this instance, to make an independent determination as to the enforceability of Chanoy Brandon’s dower claims against the estate under state law at the time the settlement was reached. Specifically, the Tax Court was required to consider the constitutionality of the Arkansas dower statute at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr. Having carefully reviewed the Tax Court’s opinion, we find that the Tax Court failed to do so.

The Tax Court’s reliance upon Estate of Barrett v. Commissioner, supra, holding that the test for determining the enforceability of the surviving spouse’s claims against the estate is whether or not the settlement agreement was made as the result of good faith, arm’s-length negotiations, was improper, because that case appears to have been overruled sub silentio by Bosch. We therefore remand for a determination of the constitutionality of ARK.STAT.ANN. § 60-501 at the time the settlement was reached.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), particularly whether an enforceable state-law interest “passes” to the surviving spouse for purposes of the marital deduction. The later amendments listed affect other subsections and do not alter § 2056(a) or its relevant function; the Equal Protection issue likewise does not change that statutory language.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-483-574.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-483-574.summary: The Court held that due process does not require clear and convincing evidence to establish paternity. Because a paternity judgment creates financial support obligations rather than terminating an existing parent-child relationship, Pennsylvania may use the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.
excerpts: The preponderance of the evidence standard that the Pennsylvania Legislature has prescribed for paternity cases is the standard that is applied most frequently in litigation between private parties in every State. More specifically, it is the same standard that is applied in paternity litigation in the majority of American jurisdictions that regard such proceedings as civil in nature.

Appellant’s principal argument is that the standard of proof required by our holding in Santosky to terminate the parent-child relationship is also constitutionally required to create it. This view of Santosky rests on the tacit assumption of an equivalence between the State’s imposition of the legal obligations accompanying a biological relationship between parent and child and the State’s termination of a fully existing parent-child relationship. We are unable to accept this assumption.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-820-f2d-923.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-820-f2d-923.citation: Harpole v. Arkansas Department of Human Services, 820 F.2d 923 (8th Cir. 1987)
us-ca8-820-f2d-923.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment due-process principles concerning familial association and recognized that parents and children may possess a liberty interest in each other’s companionship. It held, however, that Harpole did not establish a constitutionally protected loss arising from the death of her adult son, particularly where the alleged governmental interference was indirect.
excerpts: Both the Supreme Court and this court have recognized a liberty interest which parents and children have in each other’s companionship. See, e.g., Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983); Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462-63 (8th Cir.1987). Familial relationships have been protected from many forms of governmental intrusion.

The First Circuit, in Ortiz v. Burgos, 807 F.2d 6 (1st Cir.1986), divided constitutionally protected interests in familial relationships into two categories. In the first category are cases protecting the right to make private decisions affecting the family, such as whether to bear children. “The emphasis in these cases on choice suggests that the right is one of preemption; rather than an absolute right to a certain family relationship, family members have the right, when confronted with the state’s attempt to make choices for them, to choose for themselves.” Id. at 8. The second category contains cases dealing with governmental attempts to directly affect the parent-child relationship by means such as determining paternity or terminating parental rights.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-482-78.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-482-78.summary: The Court held that prisoners retain the fundamental constitutional right to marry, although incarceration permits substantial restrictions on its exercise. Applying a deferential reasonable-relationship standard, the Court invalidated Missouri’s requirement that an inmate demonstrate “compelling reasons” before marrying because the restriction was not reasonably related to legitimate penological objectives.
excerpts: In support of the marriage regulation, petitioners first suggest that the rule does not deprive prisoners of a constitutionally protected right. They concede that the decision to marry is a fundamental right under Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U. S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1 (1967), but they imply that a different rule should obtain “in ... a prison forum.

We disagree with petitioners that Zablocki does not apply to prison inmates. It is settled that a prison inmate “retains those [constitutional] rights that are not inconsistent with his status as a prisoner or with the legitimate penological objectives of the corrections system.” Pell v. Procunier, supra, at 822. The right to marry, like many other rights, is subject to substantial restrictions as a result of incarceration.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Fundamental right to marry, as recognized in Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U.S. 374 (1978), and Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967)

us-scotus-476-852.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-476-852.summary: The Court held that Texas could not deny Reed’s inheritance claim under an unconstitutional classification based on nonmarital birth merely because her father died before Trimble and she filed her claim afterward. The State’s interests in orderly estate administration and finality did not justify excluding her while the estate proceedings remained in progress.
excerpts: Although the question presented in this case is framed in terms of “retroactivity,” its answer is governed by a rather clear distinction that has emerged from our cases considering the constitutionality of statutory provisions that impose special burdens on illegitimate children. In these cases, we have unambiguously concluded that a State may not justify discriminatory treatment of illegitimates in order to express its disapproval of their parents’ misconduct.

The state interest in the orderly disposition of decedents’ estates may justify the imposition of special requirements upon an illegitimate child who asserts a right to inherit from her father, and, of course, it justifies the enforcement of generally applicable limitations on the time and the manner in which claims may be asserted. After an estate has been finally distributed, the interest in finality may provide an additional, valid justification for barring the belated assertion of claims, even though they may be meritorious and even though mistakes of law or fact may have occurred during the probate process. We find no such justification for the State’s rejection of appellant’s claim in this case.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-787-f2d-403.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-787-f2d-403.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It held that the alleged reduction of visitation and foster-placement decisions did not establish a substantive due process violation, and that Missouri’s available post-deprivation procedures provided constitutionally adequate protection for the parents’ interests.
excerpts: This court has previously recognized that “[pjarents have a fundamental ‘liberty interest’ in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983) (citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)). “That [the Fitzgeralds may have] been deprived of a constitutionally protected right, of course, does not answer the whole question of whether [they have] a claim for relief. [They] must also show that [they were] deprived of the right without due process of law.” Id.

The Fitzgeralds’ procedural due process claim is based on the defendants’ failure to provide the Fitzgeralds with a hearing prior to reducing their periodic visits with Wisa or prior to permitting Wisa to remain with her DFS-selected foster parent. We recognize the possibility that visitation and placement decisions may be subject to due process scrutiny, as such decisions may infringe upon a parent’s interest in the “care, custody, and management of their child.” Santosky v. Kramer, supra, 455 U.S. at 753, 102 S.Ct. at 1394-95.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.citation: Bohn v. County of Dakota, 772 F.2d 1433 (8th Cir. 1985)
us-ca8-772-f2d-1433.summary: The court held that the privacy and autonomy of the parent-child relationship constitute protectible liberty interests under the Due Process Clause. It therefore evaluated the procedures used to determine child abuse under the Mathews v. Eldridge framework, balancing the family interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the government's interests.
excerpts: The privacy and autonomy of familial relationships involved in a case like this are unarguably among the protectible interests which due process protects. We can conceive of no more important relationship, no more basic bond in American society, than the tie between parent and child.

Having identified the protectible interests at stake, we next turn to the procedural protections that are due under Minn. Stat.Ann. § 626.556. To assist the courts in evaluating the propriety of such procedures, the Supreme Court in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 96 S.Ct. 893, 47 L.Ed.2d 18 (1976), identified three factors:
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.citation: Horton v. Marshall Public Schools, 769 F.2d 1323 (8th Cir. 1985)
us-ca8-769-f2d-1323.summary: The court held that the school district’s policy violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause by creating an irrebuttable presumption that children without a parent or legal guardian residing in the district were not domiciled there, despite reasonable alternative means of determining domicile. The court rejected the claim that the policy impermissibly burdened a nontraditional family-living arrangement because it did not require children to live with a parent or legal guardian.
excerpts: rict court’s interpretation of the term “domicile” in the school attendance context to mean “residence”, there is no authority for so limiting a child’s domicile under Arkansas case law. See Spriggs v. Altheimer, Arkansas School District No. 22, supra. Accordingly, it is not “universally true” that children who do not have a parent or legal guardian living in the Marshall school district are not domiciled in the district (i.e. residing in the district with a present intent to remain). Since, as in Vlandis, reasonable alternative means of determining the child’s domicile exist, the Marshall school district policy creates an unconstitutional irrebuttable presumption.

3. Nontraditional Family-Living Arrangement. Plaintiffs further contend that the Marshall Public School District’s policy unconstitutionally interferes with their right to adopt a nontraditional family-living arrangement. See Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 431 U.S. 494, 506, 97 S.Ct. 1932, 1939, 52 L.Ed.2d 531 (1977). Plaintiffs reading of the school district’s policy in this regard is too broad, however, in that the district has not required minor children to actually live with a parent or legal guardian. Rather, the district has only required that a parent or legal guardian live in the Marshall school district boundaries. Thus, there is no impermissible burden on plaintiffs’ right to adopt a nontraditional family-living arrangement.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-466-429.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-466-429.summary: The Court held that a state custody decision may not remove a child from a fit natural mother based on the racial composition of her household or anticipated private racial prejudice. Although the State has a substantial interest in the child’s best interests, race-based custody classifications require compelling justification and cannot give effect to private biases.
excerpts: The Constitution cannot control such prejudices but neither can it tolerate them. Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.

A core purpose of the Fourteenth Amendment was to do away with all governmentally imposed discrimination based on race. See Strauder v. West Virginia, 100 U. S. 303, 307-308, 310 (1880). Classifying persons according to their race is more likely to reflect racial prejudice than legitimate public concerns; the race, not the person, dictates the category. See Personnel Administrator of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U. S. 256, 272 (1979). Such classifications are subject to the most exacting scrutiny; to pass constitutional muster, they must be justified by a compelling governmental interest and must be “necessary ... to the accomplishment” of their legitimate purpose, McLaughlin v. Florida, 379 U. S. 184, 196 (1964). See Loving v. Virginia, 388 U. S. 1, 11 (1967).

The question, however, is whether the reality of private biases and the possible injury they might inflict are permissible considerations for removal of an infant child from the custody of its natural mother. We have little difficulty concluding that they are not. The Constitution cannot control such prejudices but neither can it tolerate them. Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-731-f2d-527.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-731-f2d-527.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process principles to a state custody and parental-rights proceeding. It held that alleged ineffective assistance by appointed counsel and inadequate notice did not establish a due-process violation because Bruner failed to show material prejudice, and the state-court modification also made some claimed prejudice moot.
excerpts: Deborah J. Bruner brought an action under Section 1983 of Title 42 against the Director of the Nebraska Department of Public Welfare. She asserts that she had not been afforded due process in state court proceedings concerning her parental rights. The district court, the Honorable Warren K. Urbom presiding, held that Bruner had not been denied due process of law.

In federal court Bruner alleged that she had been denied effective assistance of counsel because her appointed counsel allegedly failed to interview and call material witnesses, discuss potential defenses with her, adequately apprise her of the consequences of missing hearings, develop a plan for Bruner’s resumption of custody of her son, or to object to evidence presented at the hearings in which custody was determined. Bruner also alleges that she was denied due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings dealing with custody of her son.

The district court also rejected Bruner’s allegations of a denial of due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings. Apparently Bruner missed four of fifteen hearings. The court found that her absences did not significantly affect the state court judge’s decision that Bruner was unable to care for her son’s needs; consequently, Bruner was not prejudiced, regardless of the adequacy of the notice.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-463-248.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-463-248.summary: The Court held that an unmarried biological father who had neither developed a substantial relationship with his child nor taken affirmative steps to establish one has no absolute constitutional right to notice and a hearing before the child’s adoption. New York’s statutory scheme, including its putative-father registry and defined notice categories, did not violate the Due Process or Equal Protection Clauses.
excerpts: When an unwed father demonstrates a full commitment to the responsibilities of parenthood by “com[ing] forward to participate in the rearing of his child,” Caban, 441 U. S., at 392, his interest in personal contact with his child acquires substantial protection under the Due Process Clause.

The question presented is whether New York has sufficiently protected an unmarried father’s inchoate relationship with a child whom he has never supported and rarely seen in the two years since her birth. The appellant, Jonathan Lehr, claims that the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, as interpreted in Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972), and Caban v. Mohammed, 441 U. S. 380 (1979), give him an absolute right to notice and an opportunity to be heard before the child may be adopted. We disagree.

In this case, however, it is a parent who claims that the State has improperly deprived him of a protected interest in liberty. This Court has examined the extent to which a natural father’s biological relationship with his child receives protection under the Due Process Clause in precisely three cases: Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645 (1972), Quilloin v. Walcott, 434 U. S. 246 (1978), and Caban v. Mohammed, 441 U. S. 380 (1979).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-462-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-462-1.summary: The Court held that Tennessee’s two-year limitation period for paternity and child-support actions brought on behalf of certain children born out of wedlock violated the Equal Protection Clause. The classification imposed a disability on nonmarital children that was not sufficiently related to the State’s asserted interests in avoiding stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: This case requires us to decide the constitutionality of a provision of a Tennessee statute that imposes a 2-year limitations period on paternity and child support actions brought on behalf of certain illegitimate children.

In several of these cases, we have held the classifications invalid. See, e. g., Mills v. Habluetzel, supra; Trimble v. Gordon, supra; Jimenez v. Weinberger, supra; New Jersey Welfare Rights Org. v. Cahill, supra; Gomez v. Perez, supra; Weber v. Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., supra; Glona v. American Guarantee & Liability Insurance Co., supra; Levy v. Louisiana, supra. Our consideration of these cases has been animated by a special concern for discrimination against illegitimate children.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-688-f2d-66.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-688-f2d-66.citation: Derheim v. Hennepin County Welfare Board, 688 F.2d 66 (8th Cir. 1982)
us-ca8-688-f2d-66.summary: The court rejected the substantive due process challenge to revocation of a foster-care license based on evidence of the foster parent’s juvenile assaultive offense. It held that the cited family-related substantive due process precedents did not limit the state’s authority and obligation to regulate foster children and those licensed to care for them.
excerpts: About all that can be said about these cases is that each established or vindicated an important substantive right under the Constitution, and all probably had something to do with the interests of a family unit as opposed to the state’s interests. They do not, however, individually or collectively, even arguably impose the limitation which the appellants suggest on the state’s power and obligation to deal with foster children and those whom it has licensed to care for them.

us-scotus-456-91.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-456-91.summary: The Court held that Texas’s one-year limitation for establishing paternity and obtaining child support denied equal protection because it made the opportunity for children born outside marriage effectively illusory. Although the State may impose greater restrictions on such claims because paternity must be proved, those restrictions must be substantially related to a legitimate interest in preventing stale or fraudulent claims.
excerpts: Our decision in Gomez held that “a State may not invidiously discriminate against illegitimate children by denying them substantial benefits accorded children generally.” 409 U. S., at 538. Specifically, we held that a State which grants an opportunity for legitimate children to obtain paternal support must also grant that opportunity to illegitimate children. If Gomez and the equal protection principles which underlie it are to have any meaning, it is clear that the support opportunity provided by the State to illegitimate children must be more than illusory.

Therefore, in support suits by illegitimate children more than in support suits by legitimate children, the State has an interest in preventing the prosecution of stale or fraudulent claims, and may impose greater restrictions on the former than it imposes on the latter. Such restrictions will survive equal protection scrutiny to the extent they are substantially related to a legitimate state interest. See Lalli v. Lalli, supra, at 265; Trimble v. Gordon, supra, at 767; Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U. S. 495, 510 (1976).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-455-745.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-455-745.summary: The Court held that parental rights are a constitutionally protected liberty interest and that terminating them permanently and irrevocably requires heightened procedural protection. Under the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, the State must prove the grounds for termination by at least clear and convincing evidence, rather than New York’s fair-preponderance standard.
excerpts: Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.

Today we hold that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment demands more than this. Before a State may sever completely and irrevocably the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.

At the factfinding hearing, the State must establish, among other things, that for more than a year after the child entered state custody, the agency “made diligent efforts to encourage and strengthen the parental relationship.” Fam. Ct. Act §§ 614.1.(c), 611. The State must further prove that during that same period, the child's natural parents failed “substantially and continuously or repeatedly to maintain contact with or plan for the future of the child although physically and financially able to do so.” §614.1.(d).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-ca8-664-f2d-667.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-664-f2d-667.citation: Gross ex rel. Scott v. Harris, 664 F.2d 667 (8th Cir. 1981)
us-ca8-664-f2d-667.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), which requires determining entitlement to child insurance benefits by referring to the law of the insured’s domicile governing intestate succession. It held that the former Missouri provisions conditioning an illegitimate child’s paternal inheritance—and thus eligibility for benefits—on the father’s marriage to the mother and recognition of the child were unconstitutional under the equal-protection principles applied in Trimble.
excerpts: 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) states: (2)(A) In determining whether an applicant is the child or parent of a fully or currently insured individual for purposes of this subchapter, the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which such insured individual is domiciled at the time such applicant files application, or, if such insured individual is dead, by the courts of the State in which he was domiciled at the time of his death, or, if such insured individual is or was not so domiciled in any State, by the courts of the District of Columbia.

Our inquiry, however, is not ended by a simple comparison of the statutes. In order to resolve this litigation, it remains for us to determine (1) whether the statute is unconstitutional in whole or only in part, and (2) whether the Trimble decision may be applied retrospectively so that the appellants may benefit from that decision. We shall address these issues seriatim.

us-ca8-658-f2d-641.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-658-f2d-641.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s dependency rules, including the provision deeming a child dependent when the child could inherit from the insured parent under applicable state intestacy law. It relied on equal-protection precedent invalidating Arkansas’s discriminatory intestacy rule and concluded that the child’s eligibility could not be defeated by that unconstitutional nonmarital-status classification.
excerpts: In addressing appellant’s contention that her daughter is entitled to child’s insurance benefits, we note initially that under the statute a child is deemed dependent on the deceased wage earner unless the child is illegitimate and is not living with the insured parent or is not receiving support from that parent. 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(3)(A). A child is deemed legitimate and, consequently, dependent if she may inherit personal property from the insured parent under the law of the state where that parent was domiciled at the time of his death. Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U.S. 495, 514-15 n.17, 96 S.Ct. 2755, 2766-67 n.17, 49 L.Ed.2d 651 (1976); 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and the dependency provisions in 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1)(C)(ii) and § 402(d)(3)(A), including the state-law inheritance rule for determining legitimacy and dependency. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively amend those provisions; later changes elsewhere in § 416 are unrelated, so the interpreted rule remains identical in wording and function.

us-scotus-452-412.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-452-412.summary: The Court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause to Georgia’s child-abandonment statute, which imposed a felony penalty when an abandoning parent left the State but a lesser penalty when the parent remained. The Court upheld the statute, concluding that the classification was constitutionally permissible and that its travel-related consequences did not invalidate the criminal enforcement scheme.
excerpts: Most frequently, claims of denial of equal protection of the laws are asserted by the members of a class of persons easily defined by a characteristic such as race, sex, alienage, illegitimacy, or religion. See, e. g., Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 118 U. S. 356.

In its decision sustaining the validity of § 74-9902, the Georgia Supreme Court recognized this distinction: “There is an entirely obvious difference, on the one hand, between an attempt by a 'receiving state’ to preclude or discourage inward migration from 'sending states’ of persons deemed by the ‘receiving state’ to be ‘undesirables,’ ‘non-contributors’ or ‘economically burdensome persons,’ and efforts, as in the present ease, by a ‘sending state’ to bring persons accused of crimes back from ‘receiving states’ to face criminal trial and punishment in the ‘sending state.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-452-1.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-452-1.summary: The Court held that applying Connecticut’s cost-allocation statute to deny an indigent putative father access to blood-grouping tests in a paternity action violated Fourteenth Amendment due process. Because the proceeding created a parent-child relationship and imposed substantial support obligations, the defendant was entitled to a meaningful opportunity to present highly probative exculpatory evidence.
excerpts: The private interests implicated here are substantial. Apart from the putative father’s pecuniary interest in avoiding a substantial support obligation and liberty interest threatened by the possible sanctions for noncompliance, at issue is the creation of a parent-child relationship. This Court frequently has stressed the importance of familial bonds, whether or not legitimized by marriage, and accorded them constitutional protection.

Assessment of the Mathews v. Eldridge factors indicates that appellant did not receive the process he was constitutionally due. Without aid in obtaining blood test evidence in a paternity case, an indigent defendant, who faces the State as an adversary when the child is a recipient of public assistance and who must overcome the evidentiary burden Connecticut imposes, lacks “a meaningful opportunity to be heard.” Boddie v. Connecticut, 401 U. S., at 377.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-452-18.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-452-18.citation: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981)
us-scotus-452-18.summary: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in every parental-status termination proceeding; whether due process calls for appointed counsel is to be decided case by case by the trial court, subject to appellate review, and counsel was not required on the facts of this case.
excerpts: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding. We therefore adopt the standard found appropriate in Gagnon v. Scar- pelli, and leave the decision whether due process calls for the appointment of counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings to be answered in the first instance by the trial court, subject, of course, to appellate review.
In view of all these circumstances, we hold that the trial court did not err in failing to appoint counsel for Ms. Lassiter.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-450-455.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-450-455.summary: The Court held that Louisiana’s former “head and master” statute, which gave husbands exclusive control over jointly owned community property, violated the Equal Protection Clause because it expressly discriminated on the basis of sex. The party defending the classification bore the burden of providing an exceedingly persuasive justification showing that it substantially furthered an important governmental interest.
excerpts: By granting the husband exclusive control over the disposition of community property, Art. 2404 clearly embodies the type of express gender-based discrimination that we have found unconstitutional absent a showing that the classification is tailored to further an important governmental interest.

Instead the burden remains on the party seeking to uphold a statute that expressly discriminates on the basis of sex to advance an “exceedingly persuasive justification” for the challenged classification. Personnel Administrator of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U. S. 256, 273 (1979).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-630-f2d-636.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-630-f2d-636.summary: The court applied intermediate scrutiny to Iowa’s gender-based statutory-rape classification under the Equal Protection Clause. It held that the State had not shown that limiting liability to male defendants and female victims was substantially related to important objectives such as preventing pregnancy or emotional harm.
excerpts: Gender-based classifications are subject to scrutiny under the equal protection clause, Reed v. Reed, 404 U.S. 71, 75, 92 S.Ct. 251, 253, 30 L.Ed.2d 225 (1971), including those classifications which discriminate against men. Orr v. Orr, 440 U.S. 268, 279, 99 S.Ct. 1102, 1111, 59 L.Ed.2d 306 (1979).

The state contends that the statutory rape provisions of § 698.1 had, in essence, two objectives; protecting certain young, unmarried females from unwanted pregnancies and from the possibly traumatic emotional effects of sexual intercourse with an older man who may wield undue influence oyer her. Although the state has provided no actual evidence of the statute’s purpose, it seems apparent from the face of the statute that those were the objectives intended.

In this case, the general doubts expressed by the First Circuit regarding a pregnancy rationale are reinforced by the peculiar structure of the Iowa statute. That statute superimposes strict age limitations upon its gender distinction, thereby excluding from punishment the class of males most likely to have intercou
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-446-142.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-446-142.citation: Wengler v. Druggists Mutual Insurance, 446 U.S. 142 (1980)
us-scotus-446-142.summary: The Court held that Missouri’s workers’ compensation survivor-benefit scheme violated the Fourteenth Amendment because it presumed dependency for widows but required widowers to prove incapacity or dependency. The gender-based distinction was not substantially related to an important governmental objective.
excerpts: The Missouri law, as the Missouri courts recognized, also discriminates against men who survive their employed wives’ dying in work-related accidents. To receive benefits, the surviving male spouse must prove his incapacity or dependency. The widow of a deceased wage earner, in contrast, is presumed dependent and is guaranteed a weekly benefit for life or until remarriage.

However the discrimination is described in this case, our precedents require that gender-based discriminations must serve important governmental objectives and that the discriminatory means employed must be substantially related to the achievement of those objectives. Califano v. Westcott, 443 U. S. 76, 85 (1979); Orr v. Orr, 440 U. S. 268, 279 (1979); Califano v. Webster, 430 U. S. 313, 316-317 (1977); Craig v. Boren, 429 U. S. 190, 197 (1976).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-608-f2d-307.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-608-f2d-307.summary: The court held that a parent’s presence at a termination hearing does not, by itself, establish constitutionally adequate notice. Applying procedural due process principles, it required notice stating the hearing’s date, time, and place, the proceeding’s purpose and possible consequences, the factual basis for the proposed commitment, and the governing legal standard.
excerpts: A finding that the parents were present at the hearing does not necessarily mean that the notice complied with procedural due process. The procedural due process requirements for parental rights termination hearings were announced in Alsager v. District Court of Polk County, 406 F.Supp. 10, 24-25 (S.D. Iowa 1975), aff’d, 545 F.2d 1137 (8th Cir. 1976). The notice requirements outlined in In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1, 87 S.Ct. 1428, 18 L.Ed.2d 527 (1967) were applied to parental termination hearings in Alsager.

notice should include the date, time and place of the hearing; a clear statement of the purpose of the proceedings and the possible consequences to the subject thereof; the alleged factual basis for the proposed commitment; and a statement of the legal standard upon which commitment is authorized.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-442-584.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-442-584.summary: The Court held that a child has a substantial liberty interest in avoiding unnecessary confinement for mental-health treatment, but that interest is ordinarily intertwined with the parents’ interests and responsibilities for the child’s welfare. Applying due-process balancing, the Court upheld Georgia’s voluntary-commitment scheme because parental authority and professional evaluation provided sufficient protection against arbitrary commitment without a mandatory adversary hearing.
excerpts: It is not disputed that a child, in common with adults, has a substantial liberty interest in not being confined unnecessarily for medical treatment and that the state’s involvement in the commitment decision constitutes state action under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Our jurisprudence historically has reflected Western civilization concepts of the family as a unit with broad parental authority over minor children. Our cases have consistently followed that course; our constitutional system long ago rejected any notion that a child is “the mere creature of the State” and, on the contrary, asserted that parents generally “have the right, coupled with the high duty, to recognize and prepare [their children] for additional obligations.” Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U. S. 510, 535 (1925).

In applying these criteria, we must consider first the child’s interest in not being committed. Normally, however, since this interest is inextricably linked with the parents’ interest in and obligation for the welfare and health of the child, the private interest at stake is a combination of the child’s and parents’ concerns. Next, we must examine the State’s interest in the procedures it has adopted for commitment and treatment of children. Finally, we must consider how well Georgia’s procedures protect against arbitrariness in the decision to commit a child to a state mental hospital.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-scotus-442-640.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-442-640.citation: Secretary of Public Welfare v. Institutionalized Juveniles, 442 U.S. 640 (1979)
us-scotus-442-640.summary: The Court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause to Pennsylvania’s procedures for the voluntary institutionalization of children for mental-health treatment. It held that parental consent does not eliminate the child’s liberty interest and that an independent neutral factfinder must determine whether statutory medical-admission requirements are satisfied, with periodic review of the child’s continuing need for commitment.
excerpts: We conclude .that the risk of error inherent in the parental decision to have a child institutionalized for mental health care is sufficiently great that some kind of inquiry should be made by a ‘neutral factfinder’ to determine whether the statutory requirements for admission are satisfied. . . . That inquiry must carefully probe the child’s background using all available sources, including, but not limited to, parents, schools, and other social agencies.

Of course, the review must also include an interview with the child. It is necessary that the decision-maker have the authority to refuse to admit any child who does not satisfy the medical standards for admission. Finally, it is necessary that the child’s continuing need for commitment be reviewed periodically by a similarly independent procedure.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Pennsylvania Mental Health Procedures Act of 1976, § 201

us-scotus-441-347.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-441-347.summary: The Court upheld Georgia’s restriction allowing an unmarried biological father to sue for the wrongful death of his child only if he had legitimated the child. The classification was not invidious discrimination based on illegitimacy or sex because it furthered legitimate interests in establishing paternity and preventing fraudulent or duplicative claims, and was rationally related to those interests.
excerpts: With these principles in mind, it is clear that the Georgia statute does not invidiously discriminate against the appellant simply because he is of the male sex. The fact is that mothers and fathers of illegitimate children are not similarly situated. Under Georgia law, only a father can by voluntary unilateral action make an illegitimate child legitimate. Unlike the mother of an illegitimate child whose identity will rarely be in doubt, the identity of the father will frequently be unknown. Lalli v. Lalli, 439 U. S. 259.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

us-scotus-441-380.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-441-380.summary: The Court held that New York Domestic Relations Law § 111 violated the Fourteenth Amendment because it categorically gave unmarried mothers, but not unmarried fathers with substantial parental relationships, the power to block adoption by withholding consent. The gender distinction was not substantially related to the State’s asserted interests in facilitating adoption and identifying appropriate consent requirements.
excerpts: The appellant, Abdiel Caban, challenges the constitutionality of § 111 of the New York Domestic Relations Law (McKinney 1977), under which two of his natural children were adopted by their natural mother and stepfather without his consent. We find the statute to be unconstitutional, as the distinction it invariably makes between the rights of unmarried mothers and the rights of unmarried fathers has not been shown to be substantially related to an important state interest.

In sum, we believe that § 111 is another example of “over-broad generalizations” in gender-based classifications. See Califano v. Goldfarb, 430 U. S. 199, 211 (1977); Stanton v. Stanton, 421 U. S. 7, 14-15.(1975). The effect of New York’s classification is to discriminate against unwed fathers even when their identity is known and they have manifested a significant paternal interest in the child. The facts of this case illustrate the harshness of classifying unwed fathers as being invariably less qualified and entitled than mothers to exercise a concerned judgment as to the fate of their children.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-440-268.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-440-268.summary: The Court held that Alabama’s alimony statutes, which authorized courts to require husbands but not wives to pay alimony, violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. Sex was not an adequate proxy for need or a valid means of compensating women for marital discrimination where individualized financial hearings were available.
excerpts: The question presented is the constitutionality of Alabama alimony statutes which provide that husbands, but not wives, may be required to pay alimony upon divorce. On February 26, 1974, a final decree of divorce was entered, dissolving the marriage of William and Lillian Orr. That decree directed appellant, Mr. Orr, to pay appellee, Mrs. Orr, $1,240 per month in alimony.

But in this case, even if sex were a reliable proxy for need, and even if the institution of marriage did discriminate against women, these factors still would “not adequately justify the salient features of” Alabama’s statutory scheme, Craig v. Boren, supra, at 202-203. Under the statute, individualized hearings at which the parties’ relative financial circumstances are considered ialready occur. See Russell v. Russell, 247 Ala. 284, 286, 24 So. 2d 124, 126 (1945); Ortman v. Ortman, 203 Ala. 167, 82 So. 417 (1919).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

us-scotus-439-259.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-439-259.summary: The Court applied heightened equal-protection review to New York’s inheritance classification based on nonmarital birth. It upheld § 4-1.2 because requiring a judicial declaration of paternity during the father’s lifetime was substantially related to the State’s legitimate interests in reliable paternity determinations and orderly estate administration.
excerpts: We concluded that the Illinois statute discriminated against illegitimate children in a manner prohibited by the Equal Protection Clause. Although, as decided in Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U. S. 495, 506 (1976), and reaffirmed in Trimble, supra, at 767, classifications based on illegitimacy are not subject to “strict scrutiny,” they nevertheless are invalid under the Fourteenth Amendment if they are not substantially related to permissible state interests. Upon examination, we found that the Illinois law failed that test.

At the outset we observe that § 4-1.2 is different in important respects from the statutory provision overturned in Trimble. The Illinois statute required, in addition to the father’s acknowledgment of paternity, the legitimation of the child through the intermarriage of the parents as an absolute precondition to inheritance. This combination of requirements eliminated “the possibility of a middle ground between the extremes of complete exclusion and case-by-case determination of paternity.” Trimble, 430 U. S., at 770-771. As illustrated by the facts in Trimble, even a judicial declaration of paternity was insufficient to permit inheritance.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)
N.Y. Estates, Powers, and Trusts Law § 4-1.2

us-scotus-436-84.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-436-84.summary: The Court held that California could not exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident, nondomiciliary parent in a child-support action based on his consent to his children’s relocation to California. Applying the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts standard, the Court concluded that the father’s limited California contacts and conduct did not make it fair, just, or reasonable to require him to defend the support action there.
excerpts: A father who agrees, in the interests of family harmony and his children’s preferences, to allow them to spend more time in California than was required under a separation agreement can hardly be said to have “purposefully availed himself” of the “benefits and protections” of California’s laws.

The issue before us is whether, in this action for child support, the California state courts may exercise in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident, nondomiciliary parent of minor children domiciled within the State. For reasons set forth below, we hold that the exercise of such jurisdiction would violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Like any standard that requires a determination of “reasonableness,” the “minimum contacts” test of International Shoe is not susceptible of mechanical application; rather, the facts of each case must be weighed to determine whether the requisite “affiliating circumstances” are present. Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U. S. 235, 246 (1958).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

us-scotus-434-374.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-434-374.summary: The Court held that Wisconsin’s requirement that certain parents obtain court permission before marrying violated the Equal Protection Clause because it significantly interfered with the fundamental right to marry. Regulations that do not significantly interfere with entry into marriage may still be valid.
excerpts: the right to marry is of fundamental importance for all individuals

In evaluating §§ 245.10 (1), (4), (5) under the Equal Protection Clause, “we must first determine what burden of justification the classification created thereby must meet, by looking to the nature of the classification and the individual interests affected.” Memorial Hospital v. Maricopa County, 415 U. S. 250, 253 (1974). Since our past decisions make clear that the right to marry is of fundamental importance, and since the classification at issue here significantly interferes with the exercise of that right, we believe that “critical examination” of the state interests advanced in support of the classification is required.

By reaffirming the fundamental character of the right to marry, we do not mean to suggest that every state regulation which relates in any way to the incidents of or prerequisites for marriage must be subjected to rigorous scrutiny. To the contrary, reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into the marital relationship may legitimately be imposed.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)
U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

us-scotus-434-246.court: Supreme Court of the United States
us-scotus-434-246.summary: The Court held that Georgia could deny an unwed biological father veto authority over his child’s adoption under a “best interests of the child” standard, rather than requiring a finding of unfitness. Given the father’s lack of a developed family relationship with the child and the child’s established family life with the mother and stepfather, the statutory scheme did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment.
excerpts: Thus, the underlying issue is whether, in the circumstances of this case and in light of the authority granted by Georgia law to married fathers, appellant’s interests were adequately protected by a “best interests of the child” standard. We examine this issue first under the Due Process Clause and then under the Equal Protection Clause.

We have recognized on numerous occasions that the relationship between parent and child is constitutionally protected. See, e. g., Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, 231-233 (1972) Stanley v. Illinois, supra; Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U. S. 390, 399-401 (1923). “It is cardinal with us that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents, whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause; Equal Protection Clause)

us-ca8-557-f2d-170.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
us-ca8-557-f2d-170.citation: M. S. v. Wermers, 557 F.2d 170 (8th Cir. 1977)
us-ca8-557-f2d-170.summary: The court recognized parents’ constitutionally protected authority to direct the care, custody, education, and upbringing of their minor children. It applied that principle to conclude that parents may be informed of and attempt to address a minor child’s litigation, consistent with preserving the family relationship.
